Empirical Research Plan  
“Cross‐Country Child-Penalties in Earnings and Their Contribution to Gender Inequality”  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary design: Event-study Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with individual and calendar-year fixed effects, estimated separately by country and then pooled in a triple-difference framework.  

Rationale  
• A birth—­especially the first birth—­is a discrete, well-timed shock that sharply changes parents’ labour-supply incentives.  
• Administrative panels let us observe the same individual many years before and after birth ⇒ we can difference out all time-invariant unobservables.  
• Comparing mothers to (i) their own pre-birth outcomes and (ii) fathers or women who have not yet given birth nets out aggregate shocks and life-cycle earnings profiles.  
• Cross-country variation in leave length, childcare coverage, and gender norms is exploited by interacting the post-birth dummy with country-level policy measures (policy-interaction design).  

Econometric model (country c, individual i, calendar year t, relative year k):  

log(Earnings_{ict}) = Σ_{k≠-1} β_k · 1[event=k] · Mother_i  
           + γ_i + δ_t + ε_{ict}  

where “event = –1” (the year before birth) is the omitted category. The β_k’s trace the dynamic child-penalty profile. We estimate separately for mothers and fathers, then compute  
Child-Penalty_c = β̄_post,c(Mother) – β̄_post,c(Father).  

To study determinants:  

Child-Penalty_{ict} = θ · Policy_c × Post_{it} + λ_i + η_t + u_{ict}.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
• Treated = individual is a parent in years t ≥ year of first birth (Post).  
• Focus on first-birth events between 1985-2005 to allow ≥5 pre- and ≥10 post-years.  

Control groups  
A. Within-individual: the same parent in pre-birth years (main counterfactual).  
B. Cross-individual: women/men of the same cohort who have not yet had a child by year t (“future parents”) – used to strengthen parallel-trend tests (stacked DiD).  
C. For gender-gap estimates: fathers of the same child (couple-level difference).  

Timing / key variation  
• Event time k = t – birthYear_i.  
• Policy variation: parental-leave duration, publicly provided childcare slots per child, part-time-work regulations, measured annually at the country-year level.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel pre-trends: in the absence of childbirth, earnings of soon-to-be mothers would have followed the same trend as their own pre-birth path and as the control group’s path.  
  Plausibility: Administrative earnings display smooth life-cycle patterns; visual pre-trend tests possible.  

A2. No other simultaneous shocks correlated with childbirth and earnings (e.g., marriage shocks) that differ across countries/parents in a systematic way after conditioning on fixed effects.  
  Plausibility: Some correlated events unavoidable, but couple fixed effects reduce concern.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): one parent’s birth event does not affect another non-treated individual’s earnings path used as control.  
  Plausibility: Reasonable at national scale; may fail within firms—checked in robustness.  

A4. Measurement error in earnings and birth dates is minimal.  
  Plausibility: High – administrative registers.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Endogenous timing of childbirth with respect to career shocks.  
 Fix: (i) Use long pre-trend window; (ii) exclude births preceded by large positive/negative earnings jumps; (iii) stacked DiD with “future parents” as never-treated group following Sun & Abraham (2021).  

T2. Fathers are not a perfect counterfactual if their labour supply also changes.  
 Fix: Report separate mother and father effects and their difference; robustness with non-parent controls; couple-by-year fixed effects absorb household shocks.  

T3. Country-specific macro shocks confounded with policy reforms.  
 Fix: Year fixed effects plus country-specific linear or quadratic trends; placebo checks on cohorts unexposed to the reform; difference-in-difference-in-differences (DDD) interacting Post with country and parentship.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE
library(data.table)  # efficient import

# 1. DATA LOADING ----------------------------------------------------------
files <- list.files("data/", pattern = "*.csv", full.names = TRUE)
df <- rbindlist(lapply(files, fread))  # assumes harmonised variable names

# 2. VARIABLE CONSTRUCTION -------------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    # birth year of first child
    birth_year = first_birth_year,  # supplied in data
    event_time = year - birth_year,
    post       = as.integer(event_time >= 0 & !is.na(event_time)),
    mother     = as.integer(gender == "F" & !is.na(birth_year)),
    father     = as.integer(gender == "M" & !is.na(birth_year)),
    ln_earn    = log(earnings + 1)   # avoid log(0)
  ) %>% 
  filter(event_time >= -5 & event_time <= 10) # balanced window

# 3. MAIN EVENT-STUDY SPECIFICATION ---------------------------------------
# Country-specific estimation loop
results <- list()

for(cc in unique(df$country)){
  dcc <- df %>% filter(country == cc & mother == 1)
  
  est <- feols(ln_earn ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) | id + year,
               data = dcc, cluster = ~id)
  results[[cc]] <- est
}

# Combine estimates (example: Austria)
etable(results[["Austria"]])

# 4. TRIPLE DIFFERENCE WITH POLICY ----------------------------------------
policy <- read_csv("data/policy_countryyear.csv")  # leave weeks, childcare coverage
df <- df %>% left_join(policy, by = c("country","year"))

ddd <- feols(ln_earn ~ post * leave_weeks * mother | id + country^year,
             data = df, cluster = ~country^year)

# 5. ROBUSTNESS: FUTURE-PARENT CONTROL & PRE-TREND TEST -------------------
df$future_parent <- with(df, as.integer(is.na(birth_year) | birth_year > year+10))

placebo <- feols(ln_earn ~ i(event_time, ref = -1, leads = 3:1) | id + year,
                 data = df %>% filter(mother==1), cluster = ~id)
summary(placebo)      # should show insignificant leads

# Save results
saveRDS(list(results=results, ddd=ddd, placebo=placebo), "output/estimates.rds")
```

----------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results (Priors)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Based on existing theory and descriptive evidence:  
• Childbirth reduces mothers’ earnings sharply and persistently; fathers’ earnings are flat or slightly positive.  
Magnitude after ten years:  
 Austria ≈ –30 % (β ≈ –0.35 log-points)  
 Denmark ≈ –20 % (β ≈ –0.23)  
 Sweden ≈ –15 % (β ≈ –0.16)  
These penalties account for roughly 60–80 % of the observed gender earnings gap by age 40. Differences align with more generous childcare and egalitarian norms in the Nordics.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Accurate measurement (admin data) .................... 1  
2. Parallel pre-trends visually/quantitatively verified .. 0.8  
3. Exogeneity of childbirth timing ........................ 0.6  
4. No spillovers / interference ............................ 0.7  
5. Correct functional form & clustering .................. 0.9  

Overall: Strong but not perfect; primary caveat is selection into timing of birth.
